newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania secures airport, financial crisis looms.
newsitem.headline: Albania secures airport, financial crisis looms.

text.p: Police moved to secure Tirana airport on Wednesday to reopen Albania's main gateway to the outside world but the European Union (EU) said the country remained fraught with disorder.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a member of the all-party government appointed last week, said Albania's economy had collapsed after a month of unrest and now faced paralysis.
Rebels held control of the south and threatened to form their own government unless President Sali Berisha resigned by Thursday.

Armoured vehicles and truckloads of police, each with a Kalashnikov assault rifle, were dispatched to Rinas airport, 25 km (15 miles) west of the capital. Authorities pledged to open Rinas to commercial traffic on Thursday, but Western airlines had no plans to resume flights this week.
Italian Chinook military helicopters landed twice on Wednesday at the airport, closed almost a week ago amid mounting violence.

Italian paratroopers handed over to Albanian police nearly 300 presumed criminals they said had taken advantage of the unrest to flee across the Adriatic. Many of those arriving denied having committed any crime.
The head of an EU mission probing how to help Albania get back on its feet after more than 100 deaths said no infusion of aid was possible until order had been fully restored.

"Our aim is to get aid in as quickly as possible, and we will make a priority list of things that can be done right away," Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, the head of the 11-man delegation, told a news conference.

"We are asking Albania to help us help them, they have to create a situation in the country so that the help we give them doesn't fall into the wrong hands. The police are a shambles, there are no prisons, customs or border police and hardly any army, they need just about everything."
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, head of the government overseeing elections in June, remained in Tirana, apparently cancelling plans to travel to the rebel-held south.

The unrest was sparked in the south by the collapse of shady investment schemes which soaked up the savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians. It spread to the north and threatened to engulf Tirana last week before authorities regained control.

Officials said pockets of violence persisted on Thursday, with 14 people killed by stray bullets in various towns. An Austrian television crew was robbed near the eastern border with Macedonia, an area of growing lawlessness.

An overnight curfew remains in effect throughout the country of 3.4 million, which emerged only a few years ago from decades of hardline communist rule. Emergency regulations have stopped publication of all but one government newspaper and kept schools shut for three weeks.
"The state is not able to take on the expenditure required to keep it going," Finance Minister Malaj told state television. "I must tell you that the state is facing complete financial paralysis."
The country's education minister said that, despite the country's many difficulties since independence in 1912, it had never had to shut down its schools.
Ahead of Thursday's rebel deadline for Berisha to step down, insurgent leaders said they were happy to support Fino's government but insisted it stop cooperating with the president.
Berisha says he will quit if his Democratic Party, which has ruled for five years, loses the June elections, but this has failed to satisfy the rebels.

In Italy, the government declared a national "state of emergency", recognising that it had been overwhelmed by a flood of well over 10,000 refugees from Albania in less than a week. Many have made the crossing in barely seaworthy craft.
The emergency, which will remain in force until June 30, allows access to 61 billion lire ($36 million) the government has earmarked to cover assistance to the refugees.
